claims.claim: 00 is a reading guide; where it differs from 04 and 05, those hold.
claims.evidence: Precedence rule for readers, no behavior. It names only 04 and 05, while 06 changed the primitive types that 00 §3 and §6 still list (see #42, #49).

claims.claim: A type is a collection of values and a claim about them: Int, Bool, Int -> Bool are types.
claims.evidence: Int is a primitive of core.lut, Bool an alias of a sum, `A -> B` elaborates to Pi in infer.

claims.claim: A value is a type with exactly one inhabitant (4 is { n : Int | n == 4 }); x : T reads 'x refines T'; type and value differ in how far a name is determined, not in kind.
claims.evidence: The singleton subtype works as a type: `z : { n : Int | n == 4 } := 2 + 2` is accepted, `w : { n : Int | n == 4 } := 5` is rejected ('5 does not satisfy'). But a value cannot stand where a type is expected: `four : { n : Int | n == 4 } := 4` then `y : four := 4` gives 'four has type { n : Int | n == 4 } but U was expected' (ex00_value_as_type.lut); `x : Int := 4; y : x := 4` likewise. A literal is inferred as Int, not as its singleton. The text does not say whether `y : four` must be accepted (05 §1 keeps the distinction 'on the surface'), so two readings give different behavior.

claims.claim: A function is a value of A -> B, with no separate category: it can be an argument and a result.
claims.evidence: ex00_formers.lut: `adder (n : Int) : Int -> Int := \ x { x + n }`, `twice (f : Int -> Int) (x : Int) : Int := f (f x)`, `r := twice (adder 3) 1` evaluates to 7.

claims.claim: A declaration `x : T` is a name with its base and no body: a hole (hypothesis, input, forward declaration, operation an implementation provides).
claims.evidence: A Def with body None is stored as a hole (checker add_def); api.fill and a definition in another file give it a body; `x : Int` twice is 'declared twice'.

claims.claim: A definition `x : T := t`, or `x := t` for a declared name: if t : T it is the inhabitant; if t : T -> Bool or a law over T, x is the subtype of T that t cuts out; the type of the body decides (R6).
claims.evidence: _inhabitant_or_predicate tries the inhabitant first, then the predicate; define_pending handles a declared type used as a type. A conjunction body (`R := Small & Bounded`) is exercised in test_bridge RECORD.

claims.claim: From Python, a surface that lets a type be inferred: `x := t` for a name never declared infers its type (00 L20 lists `x := t` only for a name declared before).
claims.evidence: ex00_infer.lut: `y := 3`, `f (x : Int) := x + 1`, `z := f y` load, `z` evaluates to 4; a recursive one needs a declared type (checker.py:601). No test has an undeclared `x := t`: every `name := ...` in tests fills a declaration.

claims.claim: An alias `x = t` is an abbreviation, expanded wherever it is used; it claims nothing and has no states.
claims.evidence: An alias cannot be declared or defined; `test Pos` on `Pos = { k : Int | k > 0 }` reports 'Pos: no laws'. It is not literally expanded before checking: it stays a node of the dependency graph and is unfolded on demand by delta, which is why a cycle through an alias fails (#30).

claims.claim: Dependent function `(x : A) -> B` where B may mention x.
claims.evidence: ex00_formers.lut: `zeroIdx : (n : Int) -> Fin (n + 1) := \ n { 0 }`; `eval zeroIdx 4` gives `0 : Fin (4 + 1)`. Observation: a dependent match is not supported, `dep : (b : Bool) -> pickT b := \ b { match b { true -> 1 ; false -> "s" } }` with `pickT (b : Bool) = if b then Int else String` is rejected ('1 has type Int but pickT b was expected'); 00 does not promise it.

claims.claim: Product and sum `A * B`, `A + B` are primitive and structural, with names for positions: `{ a : A, b : B }`, `< a : A | b : B >`.
claims.evidence: conv drops NoLaw labels and compares sums positionally ('labels do not count'). Exception for Bool in #12.

claims.claim: A lawless product or sum is not a new type; it is named with an alias (R4).
claims.evidence: `S : U := < a : Int | b : Bool >` and `F : U := Int -> Int` are rejected with 'names a structural type and states no law' (ex00_sum_named.lut, ex00_fn_named.lut). Only the product case has a spec file; sum and exponential go through the same branch untested.

claims.claim: Bool is `< true : Unit | false : Unit >`, a structural sum like any other (with L26).
claims.evidence: is_bool identifies Bool by its labels, conv by position, and the two disagree. ex00_bool_labels.lut: `Verdict = < wrong : Unit | right : Unit >; v : Verdict := wrong; b : Bool := v; x : Int := if b then 1 else 2` is accepted and x evaluates to 1 (wrong became true); `AlwaysWrong (n : Int) : Bool := wrong` is accepted as a law. Writing `if v then 1 else 2` directly is rejected ('true is a label of Bool...'). Labels-as-identity (test_checker_rules) and labels-as-binders (k_bool_is_sum, 04 §2) are both enforced, so the result depends on whether a value passes through a Bool-typed name.

claims.claim: Recursive data `data { ... }` is freely generated by its constructors and used only where the type is defined in terms of itself.
claims.evidence: add_data rejects a data type none of whose constructors takes the type as an argument, outside core.lut. Mutual recursion fails earlier, see #30.

claims.claim: Subtype `{ x : T | p }`: the values of T satisfying p; laws over functions are laws like any other, checked by test and recorded.
claims.evidence: A term of T checked against the subtype becomes an obligation (or is decided now if closed); `test` runs it and writes the certificate.

claims.claim: Apply and reduce: `f a`, replacing the argument in the body until nothing is left to do.
claims.evidence: whnf does beta, delta, iota, prim and extern; the call-by-need machine agrees with it on the spec programs.

claims.claim: U is the type of types; it appears when a function returns a type (templates are functions over U, L181).
claims.evidence: `Fin (n : Int) : U := {...}` and `recN (P : U) ...` work. A type-returning function whose body is structural must be an alias by R4: `pickT (b : Bool) : U := if b then Int else String` is rejected, `pickT (b : Bool) = ...` accepted. `U : U` is accepted (hierarchy is open, §9).

claims.claim: There are no mutable variables, sequence, pointers or inheritance (also §6 L174).
claims.evidence: No such syntax exists; `let p = e in body` parses to a match (parser.py:425-434), not a sequence.

claims.claim: A check is made once: a checked value gets a finer type and nothing downstream checks it again.
claims.evidence: Implemented where the value already has the subtype (no new obligation, checker.py:1447) and across runs by certificates accepted by hash. A Bool check does not refine the type: that is R11, decided and declared not implemented (05:243, 05:463). 00 states the principle without carrying that status.

claims.claim: When a program is certified, a law tested on a name is recorded in a certificate and accepted by hash afterwards.
claims.evidence: accept_certificates trusts an entry whose fingerprint hash, generators and case count match.

claims.claim: When a program runs, a condition refines the variables it tests inside its branch (R11), and a check whose evidence must outlive the branch returns the value at its refined type (refine, 05 §9).
claims.evidence: Declared not implemented at 05:243 and 05:463. No `refine` in core.lut or lib/ (grep). What exists is the mechanism R11 replaces: an obligation equal to the branch condition is discharged textually and other obligations get the condition as a precondition (add_obligation).

claims.claim: Between two different checks (a fast one and the predicate it stands for) the relation is a law certified once, so at run time only one is made.
claims.evidence: Part of 'Checks recorded in types', decided and not implemented (05:463). Nothing in the checker or runner chooses one check over another by a certified relation.

claims.claim: At the boundary of a program a check about the world refines the content it read.
claims.evidence: Decided in 05 §9 (05:439-443), declared not implemented at 05:463. The existing boundary mechanism is `run --checked` (re-testing values from externs), the deliberate exception.

claims.claim: How much the type of a result should say depends on what it costs to know it again (cheap result carries its bound; expensive one its inputs and witness).
claims.evidence: Design guidance for authors; no checker behavior.

claims.claim: Notation forms: `x : A := t`, `x : A`, `x = t`, `(x : A) -> B`, `A -> B`, `(x : A) * B`, `A * B`, `\ x { t }`.
claims.evidence: All forms parse; `(x : A) * B` gives Sigma, with the last component named it gives a labeled product.

claims.claim: `≡` is definitional equality, two terms with the same normal form, a judgement the reducer decides (also §4 L148).
claims.evidence: conv compares weak-head normal forms recursively, up to alpha, with eta and on-demand delta; it is not expressible in the language.

claims.claim: A program is a finite set of acts (declarations, definitions, aliases) plus the directives import, test, gen and operator; no statements, no sequence.
claims.evidence: parse_program dispatches test, gen, operator, import, otherwise a definition; a name defined twice or declared twice is an error (graph.py:69, :79).

claims.claim: Within a file the order of acts does not matter; dependencies are read off the names.
claims.evidence: ex00_order_operator.lut (uses before `operator` directives and before the alias), ex00_order_gen.lut (`gen` and `test` first, `import "random"` last) and ex00_order_decl.lut (`Codec := RoundTrip` and `Even := ...` before their declarations) all load.

claims.claim: The order in which acts are written does not matter, import directives included.
claims.evidence: imp/b.lut `base : Int := 41`; imp/c.lut `useB : Int := base + 1` (no import); imp/a_bc.lut `import "b"` then `import "c"`, `main : Int := useB` loads and main = 42; imp/a_cb.lut with the two imports swapped fails 'c.lut: type error: in useB: unbound name base'. The loader checks each file as it is reached, in one flat namespace, so a flat import sees whatever earlier imports loaded. This also breaks 03 §2 ('within a file, order does not matter'; 'a file sees what it imports'): c.lut sees b.lut without importing it.

claims.claim: The checker reads the whole program before checking anything (05 §2: imports included, objects computed over the whole program).
claims.evidence: imp2/theory.lut declares `Codec : {...}` and `RoundTrip (c : Codec) ...`; imp2/model.lut has `import "theory"` and `Codec := RoundTrip`. Read as one program the cycle Codec -> RoundTrip -> Codec is one object, but load_file checks theory.lut alone before model.lut: 'theory.lut: type error: in RoundTrip: Codec is used as a type but is only declared (05 R2)'. Only the case where the other file holds the bare declaration works (test_kernel.py:332). README.md:64 repeats the claim.

claims.claim: The dependency graph is not acyclic and a cycle is not an error: the strongly connected component is an object; a definition outside the loop is a branch.
claims.evidence: Function cycles and declared-type cycles work. Cycles through a data type or an alias are rejected: ex00_mutual_data3.lut (`Tree : U := data { leaf : Tree ; node : Tree -> Forest -> Tree }`, `Forest : U := data { none : Forest ; more : Tree -> Forest -> Forest }`, both directly recursive) fails 'in Tree: unbound name Forest'; ex00_data_fn_cycle.lut (`Expr` data with `app : Fn -> Expr -> Expr`, `Fn = Expr -> Expr`) fails 'in Fn: unbound name Expr'. load_object checks aliases first and pre-declares only complete definitions whose body is not a data. Not listed in 04 §7 'Not yet'.

claims.claim: Because structure is in the names, two objects with the same shape of cycle will be recognized as candidates for an isomorphism.
claims.evidence: Future tense; nothing in graph.py compares objects.

claims.claim: A name passes through three states: declared (base known), defined (body), certified.
claims.evidence: Body None is a hole, `defined()` decides definition, `checker.certified` holds names accepted from certificates; `check -v` prints certified, pending, stale, not run.

claims.claim: A name is certified when some of its laws passed test, each with a grade.
claims.evidence: The implementation certifies a name only when every law passed. ex00_some_laws.lut: `T : U := { f : Int -> Int | Good f & Odd f }` where Odd quantifies over Empty; `test v` gives 'ok Good ... [sampled, 20 cases]', 'skip Odd ... not run' and `check -v` reports '0 certified ... v: T [not run in its last test]'. 05 §1 says 'some', 05 §7 'As implemented' says 'Only passed is certified': the specification disagrees with itself.

claims.claim: Each passed law has a grade: a point, n sampled cases, or every case of a finite domain.
claims.evidence: Sampled and exhaustive (and bounded) exist and are tested; 'point' does not. point2.py over ex00_point2.lut (`sigma : Float64`, `pos : { x : Float64 | x > 0.0 } := sigma`, sigma filled with 2.0): `test pos` reports 'ok sigma > 0.0 [sampled, 100 cases]' (one case evaluated 100 times), and exhaustive reports '[exhaustive, 1 cases]'. 05 §7's 'As implemented' list does not mention the missing grade. Same gap in 01 §4 (#77).

claims.claim: A definition may use only types that are defined, except those of its own object (R2).
claims.evidence: check_defined_types rejects a declared-only type name outside the definition's object; across files see #29.

claims.claim: A hole of a defined type is a parameter (`sigma : Float64`) and what depends on it does not reduce until it is given a value.
claims.evidence: ex00_param.lut: `eval "scaled 2.0"` gives 'depends on sigma without a value'; `run` refuses without --set; `run --set sigma=1.5` prints 3.0.

claims.claim: The type is the proposition the name claims and the body its evidence.
claims.evidence: A reading; its operational content is #06 and #14.

claims.claim: Terms are names, abstractions, applications, pairs and their patterns, injections and match on them, constructors and match on them.
claims.evidence: All forms exist in syntax.py; check_match enforces coverage of labels and constructors.

claims.claim: One rule of computation, substitution `(\ x { t }) a ≡ t[a/x]`, plus unfolding a defined name and a match picking the branch that fits.
claims.evidence: beta, delta, iota implemented in whnf and in the machine; the two evaluators agree on the spec programs.

claims.claim: Executing a program by hand is choosing a definition without free variables and reducing it until nothing is left.
claims.evidence: `luthier eval` and `luthier run` reduce a closed term; a term blocked by a hole is an error.

claims.claim: Kernel formers: U, exponential and its dependent form, product and its dependent form, sum, Empty and Unit, subtype, data.
claims.evidence: Unit and Empty are non-recursive data in core.lut, allowed there by the kernel exemption of R4.

claims.claim: Int, Float64 and String are the only primitive types, filled by the interpreter.
claims.evidence: core.lut has five `primitive` bodies: Int, Real, Float64, Rational, String. 04 §2 lists Real and 06 §2, §8 add Rational; 00 was not updated (and 04 §6 still says 'Int, Float64, String').

claims.claim: Maybe A is `< nothing : Unit | just : A >` and `Fin n = { k : Int | 0 <= k and k < n }` is in the core.
claims.evidence: Both written verbatim in core.lut.

claims.claim: Primitive for performance is an extern; a numpy array is not a primitive type but a value of Fin n -> Float64.
claims.evidence: Arrays cross as the `f` of `Vec A = { n : Nat, f : Fin n -> A }`. Stale comment: src/luthier/arrays.py:3 still says '`Vec` and `Mat` are opaque types (`extern "python:numpy.ndarray"`)'.

claims.claim: Propositional equality `a = b` belongs to the proof layer, absent in version 0; `x = t` at the level of acts is an alias.
claims.evidence: `=` is parsed only as an alias at the head of an act; BINOPS has no `=`.

claims.claim: Other levels of equivalence (isomorphism, approximate equality, equality in distribution) are types on top.
claims.evidence: Library-level design; `approx` exists in real.lut, equality in distribution is open (05 §10).

claims.claim: In version 0 a law uses decidable `==` only where equality is structural; on functions it is a parameter or a component (R8).
claims.evidence: contains_function rejects `==` on exponentials, on Real and on data holding a function.

claims.claim: Program and Term as data types defined in Luthier; not in version 0.
claims.evidence: syntax.py docstring: 'The language-level `Term` datatype ... is not part of version 0'.

claims.claim: Numbers beyond Int and Float64, vectors and matrices are native types built from the kernel; numpy is their representation.
claims.evidence: Vectors and matrices are native aliases, but Real and Rational are primitives of core.lut, not built from the kernel (06 §2, §8). Stale wording.

claims.claim: The environment gives values by extern, never types (R5); `extern provisional` is the escape hatch, recorded as debt.
claims.evidence: add_extern rejects an extern of a type unless provisional; provisional names are listed by check -v and never certified.

claims.claim: Probability, beliefs and optimization are libraries, outside the kernel.
claims.evidence: They are .lut libraries with no interpreter support of their own. No pytest loads them (grep); probability and belief carry certificate files, optimization.lut has none.

claims.claim: `if` is a match on Bool, a loop is recursion, a sequence is a dependency.
claims.evidence: `if c then a else b` parses to `match c { true -> a ; false -> b }`.

claims.claim: Provenance of each piece (lambda calculus, Lisp, C++, Martin-Löf, Python, Knuth).
claims.evidence: History; the behavioral parts are #07 and #16.

claims.claim: The §8 program (N, add, doubleA, doubleB, SameDouble, doubleB') is a valid program.
claims.evidence: ex00_s8.lut (verbatim plus `test doubleB'`): `check -v` gives 'ok: 6 definitions, 1 with laws ... doubleB': SameDouble [pending]'. The exact program is not in tests; the same mechanisms are.

claims.claim: doubleA 2 and doubleB 2 both reduce to succ (succ (succ (succ zero))).
claims.evidence: `eval "doubleA (succ (succ zero))"` and `eval "doubleB (succ (succ zero))"` both print `succ (succ (succ (succ zero))) : N`.

claims.claim: The checker records the obligation of doubleB'; `test doubleB'` draws values of N, reduces both sides and writes the certificate with the number of cases.
claims.evidence: `luthier test ex00_s8.lut --seed 1`: 'doubleB': passed / ok doubleB n == doubleA n [sampled, 100 cases]'; the certificate entry has n = 100, mode sampled, the seed, and domains 'N: derived from its constructors, nesting up to 16'.

claims.claim: Proving the law for every n needs induction and is the proof layer's job.
claims.evidence: No 'proved' grade in testing.py; declared absent in v0 (00 §9, 05 §7).

claims.claim: Open: the proof layer (terminating recursor, propositional equality, verdict 'proved').
claims.evidence: Listed as open.

claims.claim: Open: a hierarchy of universes (U : U is inconsistent).
claims.evidence: Listed as open; today infer gives `U : U`.

claims.claim: Open: Program and Term as data.
claims.evidence: Listed as open (see #48).

claims.claim: Open: whether a definition carries a text field.
claims.evidence: Listed as open; Def has an unused `doc` field.

claims.claim: A law is a Bool-valued function whose parameters are quantified (`Associative A eq f x y z`).
claims.evidence: is_law accepts Bool, Law, or a Pi ending in one; flatten and peel quantify the law over its parameters.

claims.claim: Running a law is drawing values for its parameters, evaluating, and recording a counterexample if it gives false.
claims.evidence: run_law returns the first failing case as `failure`; badGroup fails with 'x = true'.

claims.claim: The unit of specification is the group of functions with the laws that relate them; functions related by a law are defined together.
claims.evidence: Objects are SCCs; `test n` also runs every member of n's object. ex01_object_test.lut: `luthier test --name isEven` runs both isEven and isOdd. No test touches object_of or the grouping (grep 'object' in tests: none).

claims.claim: With the proof layer the same law becomes a type inhabited by a proof; only the grade changes.
claims.evidence: Future; version 0 tests only.

claims.claim: The Codec object: declared over a labeled base, RoundTrip written over it, `Codec := RoundTrip & Rejects`; a model is checked against both laws.
claims.evidence: ex01_codec.lut (with `Table = Int`, `BrokenText = String`, Rejects as in 05 §8): csv passes RoundTrip and Rejects (100 cases each); `bad` (render prefixes "x") fails RoundTrip with 'counterexample: t = 1'.

claims.claim: A type is declared over a base with labels, its laws are written over that base and it is defined by them; declaration, laws and definition form a cycle, the object.
claims.evidence: A declared name used as a type is 'pending' until its laws define it; laws with no head are rejected by R2. Across files see #29.

claims.claim: The laws must touch every label; a component no law mentions is a bare function juxtaposed to the rest, and `{ ... | true }` defines nothing (R3).
claims.evidence: R3 is checked only for `x : U := { ... | p }` and for the definition of a declared type. add_alias and inline subtypes skip it. ex01_r3_alias.lut is accepted: `Semi (A : U) = { eq : A -> A -> Bool, add : A -> A -> A, mul : A -> A -> A | Associative A eq add }` (the text of r3_dangling_label.reject.lut with `: U :=` replaced by `=`), plus a model with `mul := \ a b { 0 - 99 }` that nothing constrains, `Tagged = { tag : String, value : Int | true }`, and an inline parameter type with the same dangling label. The repo's own tests rely on the gap: test_certificates.py:50 uses `{ u : Unit | \ (x : Int) { Above x } }`, whose predicate never mentions u. 05 R3 speaks of 'the body of a subtype' in general and its example is unnamed.

claims.claim: The same object can be written in one line: `Ring (A : U) : U := { eq, add, mul, zero, one, neg | laws }`.
claims.evidence: Labels without types do not parse: ex01_ring_untyped.lut gives 'parse error: line 2, col 24: expected ':', got ','. The one-line form with typed components works (r3_connected, algebra.lut:87). The text does not mark the form as schematic.

claims.claim: Two kinds of object, concrete type and theory, are told apart by the form of the definition.
claims.evidence: Both forms are accepted, but no code classifies them (grep 'concrete', 'theory', 'observer' in src/luthier/*.py: none). The behavior 05 §6 attaches to concrete types (the observers by constructors table in check -v) is absent from cmd_check.

claims.claim: A concrete type is defined natively and its values are built by its constructors; `Vec` is `{ n : Nat, f : Fin n -> Float64 }`, a value is a length and a function.
claims.evidence: `Vec (A : U) = { n : Nat, f : Fin n -> A }`, generic in A and an alias (R4); `xs : Vec Float64 := (2, \ k { 0.5 })` is accepted.

claims.claim: A theory is a subtype of a labeled base, usually parameterized; its values are models, records of operations satisfying its laws (`ringZ7 : Ring Z7`).
claims.evidence: A copy of examples/z7ring.lut: ringZ7 passes 12 laws exhaustively and badRing fails LeftInverse with 'x = true', as README.md shows; no pytest runs examples/.

claims.claim: A model can be written with externs inside the record: `csv : Codec := { parse := extern "...", render := extern "...", eq := sameTable }`.
claims.evidence: Works in ex01_codec.lut (an extern in a term takes the expected type). No test or library writes an extern inside a record literal (table_python.lut:15 uses named externs); README.md:60 shows this form.

claims.claim: An implementation is always a value; a Python implementation of a theory is a record of externs, and certifying it is testing the theory's laws on that record (R5).
claims.evidence: The model's obligations are the theory's laws applied to the record; `bad : Codec` with an extern `show` fails its test.

claims.claim: On Int and on data `==` is structural and decidable; on functions and anything containing one it is not (R8).
claims.evidence: contains_function walks data constructors; a data type holding a function has no `==`.

claims.claim: A theory carries its own equality as a component: exact on Int, within rounding on Float64, entrywise on vectors, cell by cell on tables.
claims.evidence: Setoid, exactInt, approx, approxVec, sameTable exist; Codec's eq is a `Setoid Table`. No theory over Float64 carries a within-rounding equality as a Setoid any more (float64Field removed, 06 §8); it appears as `approx tol` inside components (belief.lut:91).

claims.claim: What is certified is a law applied to values, over a domain, by a mode: one case, n sampled cases, every case of a finite domain, a witness for an existential law, or a proof.
claims.evidence: Sampled, exhaustive and bounded exist. 'One case' is not a grade (see #34). Witness and proof are declared absent (05 §4, §10; 01 §6; 00 §9).

claims.claim: A certificate records the law, the values, the grade with its n, the generators, the seed, the first cases, and the hash of the dependency cone.
claims.evidence: An entry holds hash, n, mode, seed, generators, and per law label, params, mode, cases, domains and sample_cases.

claims.claim: Two values of one type with different certificates carry different guarantees; the certificate tells them apart.
claims.evidence: Certificates are per name and per filling of holes, not per type.

claims.claim: Failure and certificate are the same record: a failure is a law with its counterexample.
claims.evidence: Failed reports are written too: ex01_codec.cert.json has an entry for `bad` with outcome 'failed' and law failure 't = 1'. Tests assert the not-run outcome in the file and the counterexample in the report, not a counterexample in the file.

claims.claim: Requirements are checked exactly on values and statistically on functions, and what was checked is kept in the certificate instead of being checked again at every use.
claims.evidence: A closed predicate on a closed value is decided at check time. A closed predicate that needs more than the checker's fuel becomes an obligation instead: ex00_point.lut with 30000 recursive steps did not finish `check` in 100 s, while 9000 steps finished in 0.3 s.

claims.claim: Characterize, do not reimplement: the laws of an object are the properties that determine its operations (R10).
claims.evidence: A rule for the author; 05 R10 says the checker does not decide it, and the 'consistent, not characterized' report is decided, not implemented (05:265). In the library, `dot : { f | DotAgrees f }` has only a comparison with dotDef. Its structural characterization (the `euclidean` instance) went with float64Field in d179c5a (06 §8), but array.lut:215-216 still says its structure 'is the Euclidean instance of algebra_python'.

claims.claim: A second implementation is not a law; where an object is characterized, a native definition and an extern are two models certified against the same laws and their agreement is a corollary.
claims.evidence: Library practice per 07 §8: leaves are declared with laws and filled by externs; `...Agrees` kept as corollaries (21 occurrences in array.lut). No checker behavior.

claims.claim: Existential laws need a witness, which version 0 cannot run; until then the witness is a component or the universal half is stated.
claims.evidence: No 'witnessed' grade in testing.py; over finite indices the existential is a fold (GreatestOf), as 07 §9 records.

claims.claim: The Store example: a parameterized type declared over a labeled base, a law over it, and `Store (S K A : U) := ReadAfterWrite S K A`.

I covered all of 00 and 01. I ran the program for each finding myself. The programs are in /tmp/claude-1000/-home-lmoffatt-Projects-luthier/8d5ce152-b54e-48c4-a388-e7a9ccb80792/scratchpad/audit/spec-00-01/ (imp/ and imp2/ hold the import cases; auditmod.py is the Python behind the Codec externs and needs PYTHONPATH set to that directory). I didn't modify the repository. pytest ran with -p no:cacheprovider, PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 and basetemp in the scratchpad: 102 passed for test_spec, test_kernel, test_checker_rules, test_sugar and test_certificates.

High findings:
(1) #28: the order of import directives matters. A flat-imported file can use names it never imported, as long as a sibling import loaded them first.
(2) #29: the loader checks each file on its own, in import order, so it does not read the whole program before checking. An object split across files (laws in one file, `Codec := RoundTrip` in the file that imports it) is rejected. README.md:64 makes the same promise.
(3) #30: a cycle through a data type or an alias is rejected with 'unbound name'. That covers mutually recursive data types, even when each one is directly recursive.
(4) #68: R3 is enforced only on `x : U := {...|p}` and on declared types. Write the rejected r3_dangling_label example as an alias and it is accepted, and `| true` passes the same way. The repo's own tests rely on this.

Medium findings: no 'point' grade, so a closed law reports 'sampled, 100 cases' (#34, #77). 'Certified' means some laws passed in 05 §1 but every law in 05 §7 (#33). A value cannot be used as a type (#3). Bool is identified by its labels in conditions but by position in conversion, so `wrong` becomes `true` through a Bool-typed name (#12). Four forms work but no test covers them: `x := t` without a declaration, an extern inside a record literal, a parameterized declared type defined later by its laws, and `test n` running the members of n's object (#7, #73, #85, #64).

Stale wording (low): 00 lists Int, Float64 and String as the only primitives, but core.lut also has Real and Rational (#42, #49). The untyped one-line Ring does not parse (#69). arrays.py:3 still calls Vec and Mat opaque externs, and array.lut:215 points to a Euclidean instance that no longer exists.

Outside my scope, seen in passing: loading a copy of examples/z7ring.lut reports algebra.lut's certificates as stale ('the code of its cone changed') at b15f2a1. The R4 error for a parameterized type suggests `write P = A * A`, which drops the binder.
